explainer_before: Earhart constructed a homemade ramp on her family tool shed and emerged from her first flight saying, 'Oh, Pidge, it's just like flying!' This is a true story.
Born in eighteen ninety-seven, Amelia grew up exploring her neighborhood, climbing trees, and hunting rats with a rifle.
During Christmas vacation in nineteen seventeen, she visited Toronto and saw wounded soldiers returning from the war.
She worked at Spadina Military Hospital, where she heard stories from military pilots and developed an interest in flying.
In nineteen twenty-eight, Earhart became the first woman to cross the Atlantic by airplane as a passenger.
By nineteen thirty-two, she made the first nonstop solo transatlantic flight by a woman, earning the Distinguished Flying Cross.
On July second, nineteen thirty-seven, Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan disappeared over the Pacific Ocean.
Declared dead in nineteen thirty-nine, no trace of them was ever found after an extensive search.
Her childhood dream of flying ultimately ended in the vast, silent depths of the Pacific.
